scope: Normalisation only, shared between the PHP and JavaScript suites. Each case is a value as a customer might type it and the value the store must keep. Whether a document is *valid* is not decided here and must not be inferred from these vectors: check digits are WCCS-028's contract, fixed against the official sources, and several documents below have deliberately arbitrary digits.
why: The vectors that matter are the ones where the obvious implementation is wrong. A normaliser written as preg_replace( '/\D/', '', $value ) passes the first case of every document and fails the rest: it truncates an alphanumeric CNPJ into a different number, turns a CPF typed with a letter into a valid CPF nobody typed, and destroys the leading zeros of a postcode. ADR-0003 forbids that expression on this path.

br.cpf.why: the punctuation the CPF is written with is removed
a leading zero is part of the document and is never truncated
surrounding whitespace is spacing, not data
an illegal character is kept so the validator can refuse it; discarding it would turn a wrong document into a valid one

br.cnpj.why: the alphanumeric format: twelve alphanumeric positions and two check digits, letters preserved
lowercase and uppercase are the same document; ADR-0003 fixes the stored form as uppercase
already unformatted alphanumeric values are unchanged
two leading zeros survive: a CNPJ is never a number
an unrecognised character is kept, not cleaned away until the value looks valid

br.cep.why: the postcode is eight digits and the first is often a zero
a dot is not part of the postcode format but is recognised punctuation

br.phone.why: the country code survives as digits and is never truncated; a field that must accept numbers from outside Brazil is a plain telephone field, because the Brazilian presets declare a Brazilian mask and a Brazilian length, and section 9 forbids imposing one on the other
an illegal character is kept so the validator can refuse it

br.cnpj.why: one mask serves both accepted formats: the wildcard positions hold a digit or a letter

br.rg.note: No validator: the format depends on the issuing state and on the type of document, and inventing a national rule was rejected in ADR-0003. The key is deliberately absent from the registry, so a definition cannot select a rule that does not exist.

validity_scope: Canonical values, as the named normalizer produces them before a validator sees them. Valid and invalid are assertions about the check digits and the format only: a valid entry says the number is well formed, never that the person or company exists or that the document belongs to whoever typed it.

not_canonical.note: Well-formed documents that are not in canonical form: either formatted, or lowercase. They are kept apart from the invalid list because the two sides answer them differently, and that difference is a decision rather than a drift. The server validates the value it stores, and ADR-0003 makes the named normalizer the only thing allowed to transform a document, so it refuses one that is not canonical instead of cleaning it. The browser validates what is in the field, which is the formatted value the mask produced, so it removes the punctuation and uppercases before checking. Both behaviours are asserted, each on its own side.

cases.why: formatted: the value is not canonical, so the field contract is not met
lowercase is not the canonical form, and a value reaching here unnormalized means the field is misconfigured
